reverse_outline.summary: Why the book starts with the business: the marketplace model dictates the architecture
The three kinds of business knowledge needed before deciding what to share: model and liquidity, industry history, and capabilities and boundaries
How the six chapters map onto those three needs, and what follows in the part intro
Lead-in to the table of chapter questions and when to read each
The vocabulary this part supplies and how it connects to the Preface, Part 2 and later parts
What Veldmark's architecture team concludes in each chapter when it tests the Common Ground program against the business
Closing: the part sets what later designs must respect, and the reader should start with the taxonomy chapter

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
Introduction ¶1: Outline 'the marketplace model dictates the architecture, so the book starts with the business' matches p01's claim.
Introduction ¶2: Outline 'three kinds of business knowledge needed before deciding what to share: model and liquidity, history, capabilities and boundaries' matches p02.
Introduction ¶3: Outline 'how the six chapters map onto those three needs, and what follows' matches p03 (two-one-three mapping plus the rest of the page).
Chapters in this part ¶1: Outline 'lead-in to the table of chapter questions and when to read each' matches p04.
How this part connects ¶1: Outline 'the vocabulary this part supplies and how it connects to the Preface, Part 2 and later parts' matches p05.
The Veldmark thread ¶1: Outline 'what Veldmark's team concludes in each chapter when testing Common Ground against the business' matches p06 (chapter-by-chapter decisions).
The Veldmark thread ¶2: Outline 'the part sets what later designs must respect; start with the taxonomy chapter' matches p07's synthesis and hand-off.
The outliner marked no unit two_ideas; every unit holds one controlling idea.
Introduction ¶1: Introduction unit: states the thesis's first half (the business decides the architecture).
Introduction ¶2: Introduction unit: sets up the three pieces of knowledge the ordered chapters supply (thesis as a whole, PI-1).
Introduction ¶3: Introduction unit: the ordered six questions, each giving the next its vocabulary (PI-1).
Chapters in this part ¶1: Supports PI-1: each chapter is the one to open for a recognizable situation.
How this part connects ¶1: Supports PI-2: names the vocabulary and the later decisions that point back to it.
The Veldmark thread ¶1: Conclusion unit: shows the vocabulary turning into decisions, one per chapter in order (thesis as a whole).
The Veldmark thread ¶2: Conclusion unit: restates that the chapters set what later designs must respect and hands off to chapter 1.
p01 example (contact / qualified lead / holding buyers' money): the prose says they need different identity, trust, payment and data systems even when their search pages look alike.

p02 Figure 1 (systems on six business blocks): both flow readers read it as the foundation of six blocks introduced just before the chapters ('Clear'); its placement after the three pieces of knowledge carries its meaning.
p04 chapter table: the lead-in 'Each row gives a chapter's question and when to open it.' says what it shows, and the AC-2 reader used it exactly that way.

p06 Veldmark scenario: the lead-in 'Using the part's vocabulary, chapter by chapter (not date order), her team:' says what the bullets show; each bullet states a decision. The share-test bullet is thin (see flow results) but still states the decision taken.

p01→p02 (elaboration): 'Deciding what a group like Veldmark, with four of almost everything, should share takes three pieces of business knowledge' carries the preface's group and elaborates the claim into its pieces.
p02→p03 (sequence): 'Six chapters ask these as six questions' carries the three pieces into the six questions.
introduction→chapters section (elaboration): p03's 'The table says when to open each' and the lead-in 'Each row gives a chapter's question and when to open it.' expand the six questions into rows.
chapters→connects (cause_effect): 'This part supplies the vocabulary the rest of the book uses' states what the chapters leave behind.

connects→conclusion (example): the opening gloss of Veldmark is followed within the lead-in by 'Using the part's vocabulary, chapter by chapter', which carries the vocabulary into Veldmark's decisions as the example. The carry-over sits in the third sentence rather than the first, but neither flow reader lost the thread at this boundary.
p06→p07 (conclusion_summary): 'Together, the six chapters say what every later design must respect' sums up the bullets.
hand_off to marketplace-taxonomy (elaboration): 'Begin with [[marketplace-taxonomy]], which asks where the marketplace's job ends.' introduces the first chapter's question.

Organizing principle: both readers describe the page moving from the claim (business first) through three pieces of knowledge to six chapters, the part's place in the book, Veldmark and the hand-off, with the chapters in prerequisite order, each answer giving the next its vocabulary. This agrees with large_to_small plus prerequisite_order. Both rate every section's position 'Clear' and neither asks for a reorder (flowB's swap of 'How this part connects' and the Veldmark thread is offered as optional; the current order is called defensible). Non-material points: bullet dates out of date order (flowA 3.9, flowB 3.8; both say the '(not date order)' note prevents confusion; already ruled by the author), 'bounded contexts' vs 'boundaries' (flowA, minor), Deal-Shaped Architecture relying on the Preface (flowA 3.10, acceptable for the audience), tense switch in the bullets (flowB 3.8).

'with four of almost everything' is used at Veldmark's first mention without saying four of what (brands, countries, verticals), and Veldmark is glossed only in the conclusion. Both readers had to guess. The audience knows Veldmark from the preface, but a few words ('four brands') would remove the stumble.
results.quote: Deciding what a group like Veldmark, with four of almost everything, should share takes three pieces of business knowledge, supplied in order.

results.finding: The Common Ground program is named but never said to be (what it proposes), so 'testing it against the business' lands only by inference.
results.quote: Veldmark, the fictional marketplace group this book follows, approved its €140 million Common Ground program in January 2027.

results.finding: The hardest sentence on the page for both readers: two colons, a 'besides' clause with two exceptions, two brands appearing for the first time and an unexplained 'for neutrality'. Both needed two passes.
results.quote: Presents a capability map on 31 March 2027: **five overlaps** where brands build the same capability, besides the Poland overlap (a portfolio question) and one duplicate kept on purpose: Keybridge's distribution beside Hearthly's ingestion, for neutrality.

results.finding: The first bullet says the team 'resolves' the Poland overlap; two bullets later it is still listed as an overlap, 'a portfolio question'. Both readers re-read to work out whether it was resolved or only classified.

Brand names (Tradeyard, Motorvane, later Keybridge and Hearthly) arrive with no word on what each is. The audience knows them from meet-veldmark and flowB calls this acceptable, so this is minor; it would be fixed by the same gloss as the 'four of almost everything' point.
results.quote: where Tradeyard's cars section and Motorvane compete for the same dealers

results.finding: The share test is never explained in the body. KEY POINTS describes four layers by their two ends; the last bullet calls it 'a shared-versus-specific table', which reads as two-way, and gives no result, unlike its siblings. Both readers paused to reconcile the bullet with KEY POINTS.
results.quote: Applies the share test per vertical: a shared-versus-specific table, ratified in April 2027.

results.finding: p03 says each answer gives the next its vocabulary; p05 says every chapter but the history one defines a term. Both readers paused over what the history chapter hands the capabilities chapter. The tension is declared in the spec itself (p03 and p05 controlling ideas), so the fix starts there, e.g. by saying the history chapter hands on a reason (why a systems inventory cannot be the unit, per how_why) rather than a term.
results.quote: defined in that order by every chapter but the history one

results.finding: 'Portugal' has no owner; the reader assumes Tradeyard Portugal. One reader only (minor).
'industry wave' arrives unannounced in a long three-clause sentence; the number of waves is given only later in the table. One reader only (minor); the intro reader also listed the term.
results.quote: each brand still runs the systems of the industry wave it was built in

results.finding: The reader had to count to check that five terms fit 'every chapter but the history one'. One reader only (minor).
results.quote: marketplace profile, liquidity cell, capability, bounded context and vertical requirement profile, defined in that order by every chapter but the history one

results.finding: Liquidity (does_not_know) is glossed at first use in p02: 'the likelihood that a listing finds a buyer in a given place and category fast enough that both come back'.

Chapter-owned terms (marketplace profile, liquidity cell, capability, bounded context, vertical requirement profile) are named and pointed to their chapters, as the spec's does_not_know and non-goals intend; marketplace profile and liquidity cell also get their dimensions in p06. The intro reader wanted a definition of 'bounded contexts', but defining it is a declared non-goal and no flow reader reported it.
Preface terms (Veldmark, its brands, Common Ground, Ingrid, the failure patterns) are on already_knows; their unexplained use is recorded under flow_is_followable, not here.

The share test is on does_not_know. KEY POINTS names its four layers only by their two ends and the body never says what it tests; the last bullet's 'shared-versus-specific table' contradicts the four-layer picture.
results.quote: Applies the share test per vertical: a shared-versus-specific table, ratified in April 2027.

results.finding: 'industry wave' is on neither audience list and is used before the page says what the waves are (the table gives 'five waves' later).
results.quote: each brand still runs the systems of the industry wave it was built in

results.finding: p01 opens with a direct claim and concrete contrast; no placeholder, restated question, dictionary or dawn-of-man opening.
The Veldmark list is the spec's declared conclusion example, and p07 adds synthesis and a hand-off; not a rephrased thesis only, grab bag or 'in conclusion' opener.

p07 synthesizes ('the six chapters say what every later design must respect before choosing a technology'); the so-what (the vocabulary turns 'four of everything' into reviewable decisions) is carried by the dated decisions in p06 (liquidity rule, exit-path rule, capability map, context map), though never stated in one sentence.
'which is why the book starts with the business' calls back to p01's opening sentence.

The intro reader names the six subjects in order (model and where the job ends; liquidity and its metrics; history and waves; capabilities that outlive systems; boundaries/bounded contexts; vertical differences and what can be shared via the share test) and predicts the rest of the page (table, place in the book, Veldmark) as the roadmap promises. Only 'who owns the listing's truth' is missing from the boundaries chapter, which the intro text does not carry; the subject itself is named.
The reader opens bounded-contexts for the listing table and vertical-requirements for the one-platform proposal, as expected, citing the table rows.
The reader says the target must name the liquidity metric it protects, quotes Veldmark's rule, and says Part I supplies the metrics that later parts point back to, as expected.
